{{Short description|Genus of extinct lizard}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = {{fossilrange|110|99|mid-[[Cretaceous]]}} | image = Carinasquama rusmithii (amber specimens).jpg | image_caption = Holotype (left) and paratype (right) specimens | display_parents = 2 | genus = Carinasquama | parent_authority = [[Juan D. Daza|Daza]] et al., [[2026 in reptile paleontology|2026]] | species = rusmithii | authority = Daza et al., 2026 }} '''''Carinasquama''''' ({{lit|keeled scale}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of possible [[pan-gekkotan]] lizard known from the mid-[[Cretaceous]] (~{{Ma|99}}) of Myanmar. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Carinasquama rusmithii''''', known from two specimens preserved in [[Burmese amber|amber from Myanmar]]. Both include limb bones and a transparent integumentary outline of the full body. A swelling at the base of the underside of the tail on one of these may indicate it is a male individual. With a [[snout–vent length]] of around {{cvt|2|cm|in}}, ''Carinaquama'' is a tiny lizard, comparable in size to the smallest living geckos. == Discovery and naming == [[File:Carinasquama rusmithii (holotype details, NMS G.2022.2.1).jpg|thumb|left|Integumentary anatomy of the ''C. rusmithii'' holotype]] The ''Carinasquama'' fossil material was discovered in [[Burmese amber|amber mines in Myanmar]], after which they were purchased from fossil traders in China. The exact locality from which they originated is unknown, but it was likely from [[Kachin State]]. One specimen was purchased by British geologist Ru D. A. Smith in December 2015, after which it was shipped to the United States. Smith showed the specimen to Juan D. Daza in February 2016, and they arranged for it to be CT scanned in November of that year at the University of Texas High-Resolution X-Ray CT Facility. In April 2022, Smith donated this specimen to the [[National Museum of Scotland]] (NMS), where it is now [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen NMS G.2022.2.1. A second similar specimen was first described in a 2016 publication under the specimen number JZC Bu269, as part of the James Zigras Collection. It was CT scanned at the [[American Museum of Natural History]] and is now housed at the [[Houston Museum of Natural Science]] as specimen HMNS.PB.729. In 2026, Daza and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Carinasquama rusmithii'' as a new genus and species of extinct lizard based on these fossil remains, establishing NMS G.2022.2.1 as the [[holotype]] specimen and HMNS.PB.729 as a [[paratype]]. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Carinasquama'', combines the [[Latin]] words {{lang|la|carina}}, meaning {{gloss|keel}} and {{lang|la|squama}}, meaning {{gloss|scale}}, alluding to the multi-keeled scales seen in both known individuals. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''rusmithii'', honors Ru Smith, the donor of the holotype specimen. == Description == [[File:Carinasquama rusmithii (skeletal anatomy).jpg|thumb|left|Skeletal anatomy of ''Carinasquama'':
skull (A–D), forelimb (E, H), and hindlimb (F, G, I, J)]] ''Carinosquama'' is a very small lizard, with a [[snout–vent length]] of {{convert|1.62|-|2.19|cm|in}}. This is comparable to the smallest modern geckos, which are in the genus ''[[Sphaerodactylus]]'' (e.g., ''[[Sphaerodactylus ariasae|S. ariasae]]'', ''[[Virgin Islands dwarf sphaero|S. parthenopion]]'', and ''[[Guantanamo collared sphaero|S. schwartzi]]''). The body of ''Carinasquama'' is depressed, and the tail is about the length of the body. The scales are widely spaced and arranged in rings covering the body, with each scale having between four and six parallel keels. The hindlimb digits are long and slender. While most of both specimens are just hollow body outlines, both retain articulated bones in the limbs, and the paratype has several skull bones. These include a left [[premaxilla]] (tooth-bearing bone at the front of the snout), which has seven tooth positions, while the [[maxilla]] (primary tooth-bearing bone of the upper jaw) has about 25 tooth positions. The [[dentary]] (main lower jaw bone) has around 24 positions, the teeth of which are well-spaced and mostly straight. === Classification and relationships === [[File:Carinasquama rusmithii (referred specimen details, HMNS.PB.729).jpg|thumb|Integumentary anatomy of the ''C. rusmithii'' paratype, including the hand (C–D), foot (F), and head (G)]] ''Carinasquama'' shares several features of the integument with modern [[gekkota]]ns (geckos). These include a missing frontal scale and frontoparietal scale, and the presence of homogeneous cephalic scales that are small and granular. Furthermore, the scales are largely consistent in size across the body, and the scales are separated by interstitial skin. As in most gekkotans except those in the family [[Eublepharidae]] (eyelid geckos), it lacks eyelids, the eyes instead being covered by a fused scale ([[brille]]). Gekkota is the clade comprising all living geckos and their immediate extinct relatives. The extinct taxa outside of this group but more closely related to geckos than any other living lizard group are part of [[Crown_group#Pan-group|Pan]]-Gekkota (also called [[Gekkonomorpha]]). Unlike the general gekkonomorph condition, but similar to ''[[Ardeosaurus]]'' and ''[[Eichstaettisaurus]]'' (which some researchers regard as gekkonomorphs), the premaxillae are paired. A [[parietal eye]] is not visible in the known ''Carinasquama'' specimens, suggesting a parietal foramen in the skull was not present, contrasting with the aforementioned gekkonomorphs and ''[[Limnoscansor]]'', ''[[Helioscopos]]'', and ''[[Norellius]]''. The second [[Phalanx bone|phalanx]] of the fourth manual (hand) digit is shortened, a feature shared with gekkotans and [[anole]]s. The astragalocalcaneum (an ankle bone formed by the fusion of the [[Talus bone|astragalus]] and [[calcaneus]]) has an enlarged process facing outward, a feature seen in gekkotans but not other squamates. The adhesive toe pads characteristic of modern geckos are not present in ''Carinasquama''. == Paleobiology == The toe claws of ''Carinasquama'' are small and not recurved, and the penultimate phalanges are not arcuate (curved). This contrasts with the arcuate penultimate phalanges of modern [[scansorial]] geckos (those adapted to climbing). This implies ''Carinasquama'' was instead a more [[terrestrial animal]]. === Sex identification === [[File:Carinasquama rusmithii and Sphaerodactylus macrolepis (cloacal region comparison).jpg|thumb|Cloaca region of ''Carinasquama'' (right) compared to female (left) and male (center) ''[[Sphaerodactylus macrolepis]]'']] [[File:Carinasquama rusmithii (life restoration, mating).jpg|thumb|upright|[[Life restoration]] of two ''Carinasquama'' individuals mating]] Identifying the sex of fossil animals is often impossible due to the lack of preserved soft tissues, especially those confidently correlated to sex. The holotype of ''C. rusmithii'' preserves a swollen region [[Anatomical terms of location#Anterior and posterior|posterior]] (toward the rear) to the [[cloaca]]. Daza and colleagues interpreted this as a hemipenal bulge, a feature seen in many [[Neontology|extant]] male lizards. This implies the presence of the paired [[Sex organ|copulatory organs]] ([[hemipenes]]) that, among other features, distinguish male squamates from females. A hemipenal bulge is not observable in the paratype specimen. == See also == * [[Paleobiota of Burmese amber]] * ''[[Cretaceogekko]]'' – an extinct contemporary gecko == References == {{Reflist|refs= {{Cite journal |last1=Daza |first1=Juan D. |last2=Selling |first2=Emily G. |last3=Jenkins |first3=Kelsey M. |last4=Stanley |first4=Edward L. |last5=Doucet |first5=Daniel S. |last6=Fotanarrosa |first6=Gabriela |last7=Bauer |first7=Aaron M. |date=2026-08-07 |title=Evidence of male anatomy in a mid-Cretaceous Burmese miniaturised amber gecko |journal=[[Swiss Journal of Palaeontology]] |volume=145 |pages=785–799 |doi=10.3897/sjp.145.188227 |issn=1664-2384 |doi-access=free}} {{Cite journal |last=Daza |first=Juan D. |last2=Stanley |first2=Edward L. |last3=Wagner |first3=Philipp |last4=Bauer |first4=Aaron M. |last5=Grimaldi |first5=David A. |date=2016-03-04 |title=Mid-Cretaceous amber fossils illuminate the past diversity of tropical lizards |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.1501080 |journal=[[Science Advances]] |language=en |volume=2 |issue=3 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.1501080 |issn=2375-2548 |pmc=4783129 |pmid=26973870 |doi-access=free}} {{cite journal |last1=Meyer |first1=Dalton |last2=Brownstein |first2=Chase D. |last3=Jenkins |first3=Kelsey M. |last4=Gauthier |first4=Jacques A. |title=A Morrison stem gekkotan reveals gecko evolution and Jurassic biogeography |date=2023-11-29 |journal=[[Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences]] |volume=290 |issue=2011 |pmid=38018104 |pmc=10685121 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2023.2284 |doi-access=free}} }} {{Extinct squamates|G.}} {{Taxonbar|from1=Q140466707|from2=Q140466708}} [[Category:Scincogekkonomorpha]] [[Category:Cretaceous lizards]] [[Category:Prehistoric lizard genera]] [[Category:Cretaceous reptiles of Asia]] [[Category:Fossils of Myanmar]] [[Category:Fossil taxa described in 2026]] [[Category:Taxa named by Juan D.
